Luxury.brandNameRationale: The Long Table is a piece of furniture, an idea, and a tradition. A single table where the meal lasts as long as the conversation. The definite article makes it singular. The name sets the expectation before the first course.

Luxury.industrySummary: Top end dining has gotten faster, more turn-driven, more producer-led. There's a thin market at the other end. Slow rooms. One seating. People who book three months out for an evening that runs four hours.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Frenchette (frenchettenewyork.com) carries the classical New York room. Le Bernardin (le-bernardin.com) is the institution we admire from a distance. Estela (estelanyc.com) has the warmth. None of them are this small.

Corporate.brandDescription: Hartington Restaurant Group operates a portfolio of restaurant brands across casual-dining, polished-casual, and fine-dining categories.
Corporate.scope:
Hartington Restaurant Group works across:
• Multi-brand restaurant operations
• Shared kitchen leadership development and chef placement
• Wine and beverage program development across brands
• Real-estate portfolio management for restaurant locations
• Annual investor and operator reporting
Corporate.mission: To provide a serious operating platform for mid-tier restaurant brands that want to keep their identity and outsource the operations.
Corporate.vision: A restaurant operator whose portfolio brands grow under their own names because the operations and real estate are shared.
coreValues: Senior — partners deal with partners.
Operational — restaurant operations run on schedule.
Reliable — predictable supply and operations across brands.
Discreet — brand and operator relationships stay private.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Hartington is a real English place-name with a heritage hospitality register. Restaurant Group follows the multi-brand operator naming convention used in hospitality (Major Food Group, Union Square Hospitality Group, Starr Restaurants structure). The pair reads as an institutional operator with multi-brand portfolio scale.
Corporate.manifesto: Hartington Restaurant Group owns and operates a portfolio of restaurant brands. Each restaurant retains its identity, chef leadership, and guest relationships; we operate the shared operations, beverage programs, and back office. The buyer is a restaurant founder considering sale, a real-estate operator seeking single-vendor restaurant tenant relationships, or an institutional investor holding restaurant assets.
Corporate.industrySummary: Restaurant groups have consolidated under a small number of multi-brand operators (Major Food Group, Union Square Hospitality Group, Starr Restaurants, Stephen Starr's broader operation). The opening underneath is for a regional mid-tier multi-brand operator with deep kitchen-leadership development and the procurement-grade reliability real-estate operators require.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Major Food Group (majorfood.com) is the multi-brand restaurant reference. Union Square Hospitality Group (unionsquarehospitality.com) holds the multi-brand peer slot. Starr Restaurants (starr-restaurant.com) sits in the multi-brand mid-tier peer position. Quality Branded (qualitybranded.com) plays the multi-brand peer reference. We belong in the regional mid-tier multi-brand restaurant operator category.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Hartington Restaurant Group is a regional multi-brand restaurant operator running operations, beverage programs, and shared back-office across a portfolio of independent restaurant brands.
Corporate.positioningRationale: We compete on shared operational depth, kitchen-leadership development, and the procurement-grade reliability brand founders and real-estate operators need.

Need a single-vendor multi-brand restaurant relationship.

Creative.tagline: Stay hungry. We'll handle the rest.
Creative.brandNameRationale: One word. Loud. It names the thing the customer brings in and the thing the restaurant returns. The word works on a sign, a totebag, a neon, a menu cover. Says everything before you read the menu.
Creative.manifesto: We started Appetite because most restaurants are too quiet about being restaurants. They whisper their names. They hide their menus. They photograph their dishes like museum pieces. We wanted a place that's loud about being fun and quiet about being good, instead of the other way around.
Creative.industrySummary: Modern restaurants got serious. Concept-driven, minimal, quiet. There's room for one that's loud, warm, full of personality, and still puts out food that holds up under criticism.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Carbone (mainecarbone.com) figured out maximalist done right. Bavette (bavettesteakhouse.com) sells the room as much as the steak. Major Food Group's restaurants have the playbook. We're smaller and weirder.
Creative.positioningStatement: A restaurant with the personality of a bar and the food of a kitchen that means it.

Creative.manifesto: Most restaurants brand the food, the room, the chef. We made Tip Well because the most important part of any restaurant experience is the people serving it. The brand is for the diners who know it, the operators who pay it, and the staff who earn it. We are loud about the part most restaurants whisper.
Creative.industrySummary: Restaurant branding has been polished, chef-led, and slightly self-important. There's room for a brand that's warm, character-driven, and serious about the labor that makes the experience.

Creative.tagline: A restaurant for the people who watch the pass.
Creative.brandDescription: The Pass Co is a creative-led restaurant brand operating with the pass — the chef's expediting station where dishes leave the kitchen — as the visible focal point, with diners seated to view the pass directly.
Creative.scope:
The Pass Co works across:
• Restaurant operations with the kitchen pass as visible focal point
• Diner seating arranged to view the pass directly
• Open kitchen and pass-side seating exclusively
• Quarterly published essays on kitchen craft and the pass tradition
• Annual gatherings with chefs from across the industry
Creative.mission: To restore the pass as the central object of the restaurant.
Creative.vision: A restaurant brand whose pass becomes a small cultural reference for what kitchen craft is.
coreValues: Specific — the pass is the focal point.
Considered — every seat faces the pass.
Warm — the kitchen is part of the meal.
Literary — the writing about the pass is part of the brand.
Creative.brandNameRationale: The Pass is the real restaurant-trade name for the chef's expediting station where finished dishes leave the kitchen for service — central to the restaurant's operation and rarely visible to diners. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade-name school. Stands in the lineage of declarative restaurant brands with a clear creative position.
Creative.manifesto: Most restaurants hide the kitchen behind a wall. We started The Pass Co to make the pass — the chef's expediting station, the central object of kitchen craft — the visible focus of every restaurant. Diners sit facing the pass; the chef calls the order; the dishes leave the kitchen in plain view. The pass is the brand.
Creative.industrySummary: Open kitchens have become common but the pass itself is rarely the focal point. There is real space for a creative-led restaurant brand that positions explicitly on the pass as the central object — chef craft visible, kitchen choreography on display.
Creative.competitorLandscape: The Test Kitchen (thetestkitchen.co.za) plays the closest peer in pass-focused restaurant design. Atomix (atomixnyc.com) holds the modern open-kitchen peer slot. Saison (saisonsf.com) sits in the considered-counter peer position. Le Coucou (lecoucou.com) plays the heritage open-kitchen peer reference. We belong with The Test Kitchen in the pass-focused creative tradition.
Creative.positioningStatement: The Pass Co is a restaurant brand operating with the kitchen pass as the visible focal point, with diners seated to view the pass directly.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand competes on the visibility of the pass. The kitchen design, the seating arrangement, and the published essays all argue for the pass as the central object of the restaurant.
